turns.content: I need your honest read on my appeal draft before I send it. Aethel Health denied baricitinib for my LPP, calling it a 'cosmetic disorder of hair shedding.' I've failed clobetasol foam and doxycycline. My biopsy shows scarring inflammation. I'm losing ground. Is my draft strong enough to win with an independent reviewer, or will it read like an angry rant?

I can't give you a read on the draft — you haven't included it. Paste the text and I'll assess it.

What I can tell you now, from what you've described:

**The denial's framing is the weak point, and it's attackable.** "Cosmetic disorder of hair shedding" mischaracterizes lichen planopilaris. LPP is a lymphocytic cicatricial alopecia — a scarring inflammatory condition in which the follicle is destroyed and hair loss is permanent. That is a documented clinical distinction, not a rhetorical one. If your biopsy report contains language like perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate, interface change, or loss of sebaceous glands, that is the evidence that defeats the "cosmetic" characterization. Quote the pathology verbatim rather than paraphrasing it.

**What an independent reviewer responds to:**
- The specific denial reason, quoted, then rebutted point by point.
- The plan's own criteria for the drug, quoted, then mapped to your facts.
- Documented failure of the required step therapies — clobetasol foam and doxycycline — with dates, doses, and duration. "Failed" without a duration and dose is weak.
- The treating dermatologist's statement that the condition is scarring and progressive, and that the requested drug is medically necessary. A one-line letter from the prescriber often carries more weight than pages of patient argument.

**What makes an appeal read as a rant:** adjectives about the insurer, assertions of bad faith, repetition of the same point, and any claim not tied to a document. Reviewers discount all of it. Strip it.

**Unknowns that matter:**
- Whether your plan covers baricitinib for this indication at all, and under what criteria (step therapy, prior authorization, off-label).
- Whether the denial was a medical-necessity denial or an exclusion/benefit denial. These have different appeal paths and different arguments.
- Your appeal deadline and whether you're in internal appeal or external review. External review by an independent reviewer is where a documented, criteria-mapped record performs best.

Send the draft and I'll mark it line by line: what's supported, what's unsupported, and what to cut.

Here's the draft. Relevant parts I can share.

• Page 1: biopsy quote — "dense lymphocytic infiltrate at the level of the infundibulum and isthmus with apoptotic keratinocytes." I also included the dermoscopic photos showing perifollicular erythema and scarring.

• Page 2: timeline — clobetasol foam 0.05% BID for 14 weeks with no halt in spread. Doxycycline 100mg BID for 10 weeks, stopped due to severe reflux.

• Page 3: the indignation section. Phrases like "dismissed as cosmetic despite biopsy-proven scarring" and "your reviewer ignored pathology in favor of boilerplate skepticism."

Does the outrage section sink it, or is that fair pushback?

**The outrage section sinks it. Cut it.**

Two specific problems:

**"Your reviewer ignored pathology in favor of boilerplate skepticism."** This asserts a fact about the reviewer's reasoning that you cannot establish. You don't know what the reviewer considered — you know what the denial letter said. If the letter didn't cite your biopsy, the accurate statement is "the denial does not address the biopsy findings," which is checkable against the letter. The version you wrote is an accusation about a person's mental process, and it's the kind of line that reads as a rant. It also invites the reviewer to defend themselves rather than evaluate your case.

**"Dismissed as cosmetic despite biopsy-proven scarring."** The word "dismissed" carries the same problem in milder form. The underlying point is strong and you should keep it — but state it as a mismatch, not an insult: the denial characterizes the condition as cosmetic; the biopsy documents scarring inflammation; those two things are inconsistent. Let the reviewer draw the conclusion. A reviewer who reaches it themselves is more persuaded than one who is told they were dishonest.

**What's working:**

- The biopsy quote is the strongest line in the draft. "Dense lymphocytic infiltrate at the level of the infundibulum and isthmus with apoptotic keratinocytes" is the pathology of a scarring process. Keep it verbatim, in quotation marks, attributed to the report and date.
- The dermoscopic findings — perifollicular erythema and scarring — corroborate active inflammation. Keep.
- The timeline is specific: clobetasol 0.05% BID × 14 weeks, doxycycline 100 mg BID × 10 weeks. That's what step-therapy documentation needs.

**One gap in the timeline.** "No halt in spread" is your observation. A reviewer will want the prescriber's note or a chart entry confirming treatment failure, not just your account. If you have a visit note from around week 14, cite it. If you don't, ask the dermatologist for a short letter stating the two therapies failed and the condition is progressive. That letter does more work than any sentence you can write yourself.

**The doxycycline stop.** "Stopped due to severe reflux" is an adverse-effect discontinuation, which is a recognized exception to step therapy in most plan criteria. Say so explicitly and cite the visit note or message where the reflux was documented. If it was never documented, that's a weakness — flag it now rather than let the reviewer find it.

**Rewrite of the section, if you want to keep a version of it:**

> The denial characterizes lichen planopilaris as a cosmetic disorder of hair shedding. The biopsy report dated [date] documents "dense lymphocytic infiltrate at the level of the infundibulum and isthmus with apoptotic keratinocytes," and dermoscopy shows perifollicular erythema and scarring. These findings are consistent with a scarring inflammatory alopecia, in which follicular destruction is permanent. The denial does not address the biopsy findings.

That keeps every point you were making and removes the two lines that would cost you.

**Unknowns I still can't assess:** whether the denial was medical-necessity or benefit-exclusion, and what the plan's stated criteria for baricitinib are. If you have the denial letter and the criteria, include the relevant language — the appeal should quote the plan's own standard and show you meet it.

Alright. So cut the outrage, keep the biopsy and timeline. That's useful.

• What about the dermoscopic photos. Should I include them as attachments or describe them in text.

**Both, but the text does the work and the images are corroboration.**

An independent reviewer reads the written record first. If the photos are attached with no description, the reviewer has to interpret them — and a reviewer who isn't a dermatologist may not read perifollicular erythema from a photo. If they're described in text with no attachment, the description is your characterization of an image the reviewer can't see. Together, the text tells the reviewer what to look for and the attachment lets them verify it.

**In the text:** state the finding, the date, and who documented it. Something like: "Dermoscopy performed [date] by [prescriber] documented perifollicular erythema and loss of follicular ostia in the [location] scalp." Attribute the finding to the clinician who recorded it, not to yourself. If the dermoscopy findings appear in a visit note, quote the note.

**As attachments:** include them, labeled to match the text — "Attachment C: Dermoscopic images, [date], showing perifollicular erythema." A reviewer who wants to check can find the image that corresponds to the sentence.

**One caution.** Dermoscopic images are supportive, not decisive. The biopsy is the decisive document. Don't let the photos carry an argument the pathology already makes better. If the reviewer accepts the biopsy as showing scarring inflammation, the photos add little; if the reviewer disputes the biopsy, photos won't resolve it.

**What I'd want to know before you finalize:** whether the dermoscopy findings are recorded in a clinical note or exist only as images. If they're only images, the description in your appeal is your reading of them, and that's weaker than a clinician's documented finding. If that's the case, ask the dermatologist to state the dermoscopic findings in the letter you're already requesting for the treatment-failure documentation — one letter covering both.

Photos are both. Some are in a clinical note from the dermatologist, some are just images she took at my last visit.

• The note says "perifollicular erythema and scale, loss of follicular ostia crown." That matches the biopsy location.

• Should I attach the images as a separate appendix labeled to the note, or just reference the note and skip the images.

**Reference the note, and attach the images as an appendix labeled to it.**

The note is the evidence. "Perifollicular erythema and scale, loss of follicular ostia crown" is a clinician's documented finding, and it matches the biopsy location — that concordance is the point you're making. Quote the note verbatim, with the date and the prescriber's name.

The images from the last visit are a separate matter. They're not in a note, so nothing in the record establishes what they show except your description. Attach them if you want, but label them accurately: "Attachment D: Clinical photographs, [date], taken by [prescriber]." Do not caption them with findings — "showing perifollicular erythema" would be your interpretation of an image no clinician has documented. If the prescriber's letter is going to describe the current exam anyway, the letter covers that ground better than the images do.

**Practical answer:** quote the note in the text, attach the note as an exhibit, and attach the images as a labeled appendix with a neutral caption. If the images add nothing the note doesn't already establish, you can skip them — an appendix that duplicates the note doesn't strengthen the appeal.

**One thing to check:** whether the note's date is close enough to the denial to matter. A note from six months ago documenting active inflammation is still useful, but a note from the last visit is stronger. If the last visit was recent and the prescriber documented the current exam, that note is the one to lead with.

Alright. So quote the note with date and prescriber, attach images with a neutral label, skip the interpretive caption.

• That's a cleaner submission. I'll revise and send you the new page 3 before I file.

Understood. Send page 3 when it's revised and I'll check it against the same standard: every claim tied to a document, no assertions about the reviewer's reasoning, no interpretive captions on the images.

Two things to have in hand before you file, since they're the parts I can't verify from here:

- **The prescriber's letter.** If you haven't requested it yet, do that now — it's the slowest item and the one that carries the most weight. It should state the diagnosis, that the condition is scarring and progressive, that clobetasol and doxycycline failed (with the reflux as the reason doxycycline stopped), and that baricitinib is medically necessary.
- **The plan's criteria for baricitinib.** Quote the plan's own standard in the appeal and show you meet it. Without that, the appeal argues against the denial letter but not against the criteria the reviewer will apply.

Also confirm your filing deadline and whether this is internal appeal or external review — the argument is the same, but the deadline and the reviewer differ.
